Then one day, on his way home from school, he ran into Nakayama.
"N-Nakayama..."
"Long time no see.
...Why do people kill animals, I wonder?"
"You eat meat and fish too, don't you?"
"That's true."
That was all she said before she fell silent.
Her eyes wavered, as if she were thinking something over.
(I don't have time for this.)
He hurried away from there.{p}

He went to a friend's house and didn't come home until after dark.
"You're late. Dinner's ready."
When he got home, Morikawa's mother had a warm supper waiting for him.
"Mom, this is great.
This fried chicken."
"Is it? Too bad, I'm afraid I didn't make it.
Say, that cute girl, is she your girlfriend?"
Morikawa had no idea what she was talking about.
"Huh? Who do you mean?"
"A cute girl named Nakayama brought that fried chicken over for us."{p}

That night, he went to bed early.
But he slept badly, and he woke up in the middle of the night.
He had the feeling that someone was staring at him.
"Mom...?"
There was no answer.
There was no one else in Morikawa's room.
"Just my imagination... I guess."
Muttering, he wiped away the sweat beading on his forehead.
Thinking how hot it was, he reached out to open the window, and...{p}

"Morikawa, how did you like my cooking?"
There was a figure by the window.
In the moonlight, the silhouette of a skirt stood out, swaying in the wind.
If you didn't stop to think why that person had appeared, it would have been a very beautiful sight.{p}

"N-Nakayama...?"
"You see, if you kill something, you have to eat it.
That's the responsibility of the one who killed it."
"............!"
Morikawa couldn't make a sound.
The meat in the fried chicken Nakayama had made was the dead hamster.
She took out a kitchen knife, slowly came closer, and stabbed it into Morikawa's leg.{p}
The pain and terror were so great that Morikawa couldn't even cry out, let alone move.{p}

"I have to take responsibility and eat too."
With that, she gouged out his flesh with the knife.
"Looks delicious.
Why was I ever so sad just because a hamster died?
Hey, Morikawa, what kinds of food do you like?
How about sashimi?
I love horse mackerel served ikizukuri, sliced up while it's still alive.
When I realized that, it just struck me as funny...
So how does it feel to be sliced up alive?"
She gazed at Morikawa with unfocused eyes.{p}

...The next day, when Morikawa didn't get up, his mother went to wake him.
When she went into his room, she found Morikawa lying there, badly wounded.
I hear he'd been stabbed all over... his legs, his arms, his stomach...
Morikawa was rushed off in an ambulance, and his life was saved.
That said, he's still in the hospital.
Yes, that's right.
The incident must have been a terrible shock to him.
They say he's gone a little strange in the head.{p}

Huh? Nakayama, you ask?
She comes to school as if nothing happened.
Morikawa says Nakayama did it, but the police don't seem to believe him.
This is what I heard when I went to visit Morikawa in the hospital.
He didn't seem to me like he was lying.{p}

That's the end of my story, but if you want to know more, why not visit the hospital?
Oh, Nakayama is a second-year now, but 'Nakayama' is a made-up name, so you won't find her even if you go to interview her.{p}Well then, next person, please.{p}

Morikawa got worried.
His feelings about animals and about life were just a little off; he wasn't actually a bad person.
"Let's look for it one more time,"
said one of the boys in the class.{p}

So after school, everyone split up and began searching.
They all searched as hard as they could, but the hamster was nowhere to be found.
Of course, Morikawa had killed it and thrown it in the incinerator, so there was no way they'd find it.
But the kids in the class just wouldn't give up.
Morikawa couldn't stand it anymore.
"I'm going to go look outside."
"Good idea, I'll come too."
With that, he went out to the schoolyard with a few others.{p}

"Hey, isn't that Nakayama?"
"What? Where?"
Morikawa asked, startled.
"That one up on the roof."{p}

That's right, Nakayama was standing on the roof.
"Nakayama..."
Morikawa called out to her without thinking, even though there was no way she could hear him up on the roof.
If he didn't stop her, something was going to happen.
That was the feeling in the air.
And his hunch proved right.{p}
Nakayama put her hands on the roof railing and leaned out over it.{p}

"Look ou...!"
Her body floated lightly into the air.{p}

I'm told she looked very small in Morikawa's eyes.
The classmate beside him let out a scream.
Nakayama's body slammed into the ground, and her spattering blood landed on Morikawa's cheek.
That blood, he said, was strangely warm...{p}

She died instantly, I hear.
It must have been suicide after all.
I don't know whether it was because she found out her hamster was dead, or whether there was some other reason.
If it was because her pet died...
Nakayama must have really adored that hamster.
Or maybe she shared some precious memory with it...
Some people might think, 'All that over a dead pet?'
But you never know what circumstances a person might have.
What about you? Don't you have one?
Something more precious to you than your own life...?
Well, most people wouldn't, I suppose.
Everyone loves themselves most, after all.{p}

...Shall we get back to Morikawa?
Seeing someone die made him truly feel what life meant for the first time.
I suppose he realized that the life of a living thing isn't something to be treated lightly.
But by then it was too late.
For a while, Morikawa lived tormented by regret and self-reproach.
He changed a great deal, you know.
Not only did he stop killing animals, of course, he often scolded people who left food on their plates, saying no living thing's life should be taken for nothing.{p}

...Nakayama's desk stayed empty.
No transfer student came, and no one ended up sitting there when seats were changed.
I wonder if that lonely empty seat accused Morikawa every day.
One day, he went up to the roof where Nakayama had killed herself.{p}

(So Nakayama... jumped from here.)
Thinking that, he peered down over the railing.
Morikawa stared at the ground for a while.
And then, suddenly, he climbed over the railing and jumped.{p}

...After Morikawa's death, something that seemed to be a suicide note was found in his room, but all it did was flatly set down the facts about the hamster.
Why would he leave something like that, I wonder?
Was he thinking about his own sin as he wrote it?
Or was he thinking about Nakayama's death?
Or perhaps he wanted to say that human lives are just as fleeting as the lives of the animals he had so easily killed...
Why did Morikawa kill himself, when he had realized how precious life is?
Can anyone say that his regret and suffering outweighed the weight of that life?{p}

Some people say Nakayama cursed him to death.
What's the real truth, I wonder?
Now that Morikawa is dead, it will remain a mystery forever.{p}That's the end of my story.
Next person, please...{p}

That's right, he ran away.
"Hey, Morikawa, what's wro..."
Ignoring his friend's voice, he dashed right past.
"What's with him?"
Morikawa looked for somewhere nobody would be.
And so he came all the way up to the roof.{p}

"I'll hide up here until everyone goes home."
With that, he hid behind the water tank.{p}

The going-home music played, and silence fell over the school.
For a while, he had time on his hands with nothing to do.{p}
He heard footsteps.{p}

"N-Nakayama..."
Morikawa couldn't get another word out.
She was holding the hamster in her hand as she came toward him.
Her indescribable intensity drove Morikawa back until he was pinned against the railing.{p}
Nakayama stopped, turning a contemptuous smile on him as he cowered.{p}

Then she tore the hamster's corpse apart and smeared its blood on herself.
That's not normal, is it?
Morikawa was so terrified he couldn't move a muscle.
In the middle of that terror, he sensed his own death for the first time.{p}
She started walking toward Morikawa.{p}

He died, and was released from his pain.
No doubt, for him, dying was easier than fighting back.
Even if she wasn't in her right mind, she was only a girl, you know.
Morikawa simply had no attachment to life, I suppose.
Ever since then, there have been a lot of suicides there.
I don't know the reason, though.
Maybe Morikawa regrets having died.{p}

What's Nakayama doing now, you ask?
She's still at this school.
She's a second-year now.
Yes, it's true that she was involved in Morikawa's death.
But Morikawa's case was written off as a simple suicide.
Why? Because when Morikawa died, Nakayama was in a make-up class.
Everyone who was there testifies that Nakayama was definitely in the classroom at the time.
Huh? You're asking if this story is a lie?{p}

No, it isn't. I was right there when it happened, after all.
Back then, I hated studying with my idiot classmates, so I used to study alone on the roof.
Well, I've matured as a person since then, so these days I study with everyone, at their level.
So this story is true.{p}

I did look away when Morikawa killed himself, though.
I never wanted to see anyone jump again.
Whether you believe it or not is up to you, {a}{f:|}.{p}That's the end of my story.
Next person, please.{p}

That's right, he put the corpse back in the bag and quietly went back to the nurse's office.
After fourth period ended, he waited a while before returning to the classroom.{p}

When he got back, Nakayama's class was in an uproar.
Of course, Morikawa knew the reason, but he asked,
"What's wrong?"
anyway.
"Well, the hamster that was in the bag is dead."
One of the kids in the class said that.
"How did it die?"
someone wondered aloud, but no one could come up with an answer.
So Morikawa worked up his nerve and spoke.{p}

"Nobody would expect a hamster to be in a bag, so maybe someone bumped into it?"
Everyone nodded with a look that said, 'Now that you mention it...'
Morikawa had succeeded in covering it up.
When he killed the hamster, he had crushed it to death.
And he went home that day feeling refreshed.{p}

(By tomorrow, everyone will have forgotten.
It's just a little animal that cost a few hundred yen.){p}

The next day, when he got to school, everything was in an uproar.
Nakayama had jumped from the roof after school the day before.{p}

She must have convinced herself she'd killed it through her own carelessness.
As for Morikawa,
(Killing yourself over a hamster? How stupid.)
that seems to be what he thought.{p}

On the day of the funeral, he attended too.
She had been their only daughter, and her parents' grief was terrible.
Both of them looked as if they had lost the will to live.
Seeing them like that, Morikawa understood for the first time what it means for a person to die.
He agonized over the weight of his sin.
And he decided that the only way to atone for it was to offer up the precious life he had finally come to understand... yes, his own life.{p}

That night, he went to the school roof.
He went to the spot where she had jumped, put his hands on the railing, and climbed over it.{p}

After that, strange things began to happen there.
Several news crews came to see the scene of the suicides, but afterward, the people dear to them died one after another.
I think Morikawa was trying to teach the value of life to people who enjoyed others' deaths for the fun of it.
Though it was a pretty twisted way of doing it.{p}

Since then, they say anyone who comes up to the roof to gawk at the suicide scene for fun loses someone dear to them.
It seems Morikawa still misunderstands what makes life precious.
But now there's no way to teach Morikawa that you mustn't take precious lives in order to teach people the value of life.{p}That's the end of my story.
Next person, please.{p}

I see.
It's true, there could be a tree or something below to cushion the fall, and someone might miraculously survive.{p}

You have, haven't you?
You see, I think that every human being has moments when they think about things like that.{p}

Even when your head knows you could never do it, you think about it anyway.
Do you know how that emotional mechanism works?
For example, if someone asked you what 'the one thing you must never do' is, how would you answer?
Take a moment and think about it.
...They say the answer is actually what that person secretly wants to do, deep down in their heart.
The feeling that you absolutely can't do something is apparently the key that sets off the desire to try it.
Don't you find that frightening?{p}

What would happen if you jumped off the roof of the new school building?
That thought ate away at the heart of a certain boy.
His name was Nobuhiko Aizawa.
They say Aizawa had been a perfectly ordinary person until then.
But...{p}
A pitch-black temptation had taken root deep in his heart.{p}

If someone jumped off that high roof...
what would happen?
What on earth would happen?
What would happen to the flesh?
What would happen to the bones?
What would happen to the voice?
What would happen to the people around them?
After jumping, how would it feel to look up?
How thrilling would it be to jump headfirst?
What shape would a body end up in if it hit the ground arm-first?{p}

At the moment of impact, would the blood spray onto your face?
Would it be cold?
Or would it be hot?
What would the floating feeling be like?
Would it feel like flying freely through the sky?
Or like falling into a bottomless abyss?{p}

What would it be like during the fall?
Would you regret it?
Would you be scared?
Or would it feel good?
Would you think of someone?
Or would you think of no one at all?
...
One question after another welled up inside him.{p}

So Aizawa started keeping a notebook.
He carefully wrote down each of his questions, one by one.
Then he picked out the items that seemed most important.
And finally he chose the one item that bothered him more than any other.
It was this single sentence:{p}

If a person jumps off the roof, will they really die...?
To him, this seemed the most important thing of all.
He agonized over it.
He had to see someone fall from the roof, no matter what.
And he wanted to know whether they would survive...{p}

He also thought about pushing someone off the roof.
But he came to the conclusion that trying it himself was the quickest way.
Pushing someone off would take all sorts of preparations.
If the person fought back, or if someone spotted him, there was no guarantee it wouldn't fail.
And if it failed...
Carrying out this experiment a second time would be even harder than it was now.{p}

So he decided that jumping himself was the surest and fastest way.
Besides, the idea of jumping off the roof himself was an all-too-sweet temptation.
He had to try it.
That's what he thought.{p}

Then, one Sunday, he headed up to the roof, keeping out of sight.
The stairs leading to the new building's roof were poorly ventilated, so they had a faintly musty smell.
Breathing in that smell, he thought about the smell of human death.
If he jumped and died, would the stench of death soak into the ground?
Thinking such things, he savored the fact that he was about to attempt a truly precious experiment.{p}

The sound of his own footsteps climbing the stairs one by one echoed through the silent space.
Somehow, he had come to feel solemn.{p}

When he reached the top of the stairs and opened the door to the roof, the humid summer air greeted him.
Then he put his hands on the roof railing and jumped without hesitation...{p}

...People often say that when you look down from a high place, you feel like you're being pulled in, don't they?
Did you know that's the dead lurking deep in the earth, beckoning to you?
Oh yes, you'd better be careful when you go up to the roof of this school.
Because they say Aizawa beckons.
In fact, I hear there was a student who ended up jumping because of it.
Maybe Aizawa isn't satisfied with the answer he found.
Maybe that's why he keeps beckoning people one after another, trying to learn what happens when they jump.{p}

You know, I think...
maybe what he wanted was the answer that people don't die even if they fall off the roof.
I mean, looking down from the roof feels wonderful, doesn't it?
Don't you think jumping would feel good?
And yet, if you fell, you'd die... Doesn't that seem kind of strange...?
But the reason you feel that way is that the dead are calling you.
Aizawa didn't understand that and fell victim to it, so I think he was an unfortunate person.{p}

You should be very careful, too.
If the dead only call to you, that's not so bad.
But they say the dead whose feelings are strong will sometimes come up behind someone looking down from a high place and... push them off.{p}...That's the end of my story.
Whose turn is next?{p}

As he was leaning against the roof railing, a boy came up.
At that moment, the only people on the roof were Aizawa and this student.
If he pushed this guy off now, maybe no one would ever find out...
That's what Aizawa thought.
But this was a matter that called for caution.
Aizawa waited for the boy to leave.
Having someone around would be distracting while he worked out his plan.
But the boy showed no sign of leaving.
Far from it, he said something like this:
"I wonder what would happen if someone jumped from a place like this..."
Aizawa thought:
It wouldn't hurt to have a partner in the plan.
No, he wouldn't even have to make him a partner.
Couldn't he find a way to make good use of this guy...?
So Aizawa decided to try talking to the boy about all sorts of things.
It turned out the boy loved the roof and came up there often.
He seemed very timid, the kind Aizawa could order around however it suited him.{p}

Aizawa arranged to meet him on the roof every day.
And he gradually planted his own ideas in the boy's head.
"Don't you want to know whether a person dies if they jump off the roof?"
The boy looked a little frightened, but he nodded firmly.
Aizawa pressed further.
"Isn't there anyone you think is in the way?"
The boy seemed to understand what Aizawa was getting at.
He lowered his eyes and answered like this:
"I hate myself.
Sometimes I think it'd be better if I didn't exist..."
When he heard those words, Aizawa's target was decided.
Aizawa meant to egg the boy on and get him to jump off the roof.{p}

The two of them talked about death.
Every day they met on the roof, gazed down at the ground through the railing, and talked about the world after death.
Aizawa said the afterlife had to be a wonderful place.
He wanted the boy to throw himself off as soon as possible.
But the boy just wouldn't put Aizawa's plan into action.{p}

So one day, Aizawa decided to take drastic measures.
He met the boy on the roof as usual and held out a sheet of paper and a mechanical pencil.{p}

"Why don't you try writing a suicide note?"
Aizawa suggested.
"You write a suicide note so you're ready to say goodbye to this world anytime."
Aizawa showed the boy an example.
He showed him a suicide note in his own handwriting and told him to just write it exactly like this.{p}
The boy took the mechanical pencil in his trembling hand and...
